newsitem.title: JAPAN: Merger of Hokkaido-based banks could be delayed.
newsitem.headline: Merger of Hokkaido-based banks could be delayed.

text.p: Regional Japanese bank Hokkaido Bank Ltd warned on Tuesday that its planned merger with Hokkaido Takushoku Bank Ltd may be delayed if the two cannot come up with a plan by end-September to rationalise their businesses.

Hokkaido Bank president Tsuneo Fujita was quoted by a spokesman as saying that devising a rationalisation plan would not be an easy task and that the merger could be delayed from the planned date of April 1, 1998, depending on the talks.

Analysts said they see a rift forming between the two troubled banks, both saddled with mountains of bad loans, and this may cloud the fate of their planned merger, announced in April as a way for them to overcome their financial woes.
"It seems there is discord emerging between Hokkaido Takushoku and Hokkaido," said Nozomu Kunishige, a senior analyst at Lehman Brothers Japan Inc.

"I don't think this alone will lead to any cancellation of their planned merger, but if they were to cancel the plan which is the core of their business strategy, that would damage investor trust," he said.
Some analysts were more pessimistic, saying that the merger plans could still be called off.

Hokkaido Takushoku has forecast 3.0 billion yen ($26.3 million) in parent current profits for the 1997/98 business year, which ends in March 1998, but analysts said the bank may be forced to post losses if Tokyo share prices fall.
If that happens, they added, the merger may run aground.
Shares in both banks dropped on Tuesday after news of the possible merger delay, with Hokkaido Bank ending down four yen at 140 and Hokkaido Takushoku falling two yen to end at 142.

In April, Hokkaido Takushoku, Japan's 10th-largest commercial bank, said it and the smaller Hokkaido Bank would merge as equals. Both banks are based in Sapporo, the largest city on Japan's northernmost island of Hokkaido.
Hokkaido Takushoku also said it will cease its overseas operations on April 1998 in order to become a "super-regional" bank.

At the time of the merger announcement, Hokkaido Takushoku said it had no choice but to retrench, ending its lofty ambitions of becoming a global player in banking. The merger will cut costs at the two banks and eliminate 2,000 jobs.

The merger is vital for Hokkaido Takushoku, which has long been considered the most troubled of Japan's major city banks, burdened with bad loans after Japan's bubble of inflated asset prices burst in the early 1990s.

A Hokkaido Bank spokesman told Reuters on Tuesday that the most difficult tasks for the two partners in drafting their rationalisation plans were setting up a common standard in assessing their bad loan holdings and reaching a consensus on how to deal with them.

The Hokkaido Bank spokesman said that the two banks were due to announce their rationalisation plans in September, adding that the announcement was necessary to gain understanding from shareholders and clients of the new bank.
Despite the warning from its merger partner, Hokkaido Takushoku maintained an optimistic tone, ruling out any possible delays in the merger.

"There is no change in our policy to prepare for the merger to be carried out as planned on April 1," a Hokkaido Takushoku spokesman told Reuters. He added that there was no specific deadline for drafting the rationalisation plan.

In June, Hokkaido Takushoku said it will work out a cooperative arrangement with Britain's Barclays Bank, that will aid its restructuring scheme while giving Barclays a foothold in the Japanese market.
At that time, Hokkaido Takushoku said it had not discussed the Barclays alliance with Hokkaido and that the alliance was merely a issue between itself and Barclays.
